18ez2vv: «Cuyo» links a possessor with what belongs to it: «el arquitecto cuyos planos se conservan». It goes between the two nouns and agrees with what is possessed, that is, with the noun that follows, not with the possessor. That is why we say «la ciudad cuyo trazado» (masculine, because «trazado» is) and «el barrio cuyas casas» (feminine plural).
mbjdng: «Cuyo» is never followed by an article: «cuyo el balcón» is wrong. If the verb requires a preposition, it goes in front, as with the other relatives: «la casa de cuyo patio salía música», «la familia para cuya tienda trabajaba».
1s4env5: Cover the possessor and read only «cuyo» + noun: they must agree with each other, like an adjective and its noun. What comes after is in charge.

1ixg9r2: «Cuyo» belongs to careful texts: guides, articles, fact sheets, speeches. In speech it is rarely used, and it is natural to rephrase. You can use «del que / de la que / de quien» with a different order («una casa de la que conozco la historia»), make two sentences («Es un edificio precioso. Su fachada es de 1890») or use «que tiene» («una casa que tiene un balcón enorme»).
jdfarw: What is not considered correct in careful language is «que su»: «el vecino que su casa está restaurada». And do not confuse «cuyo» with «¿de quién?»: «cuyo» never asks a question.

1em4avq: «…, lo que» and «…, lo cual»: commenting on a whole fact
pw4zra: When you want to comment on everything said before (a whole fact, not a noun), you use «lo que» or «lo cual» after a comma: «Llovió toda la mañana, lo cual retrasó la grabación». The antecedent is the whole sentence. «Que» alone does not work, because it needs a noun to refer to.
e49thl: With a preposition in front you chain consequences and reactions: «por lo que» (and so), «con lo cual» (so), «a lo que» (to which), «de lo que» (about which). The preposition depends on the meaning or on the verb that follows: «…, a lo que respondió…», «…, de lo que se quejó…».
l26dxw: Do not confuse this use with «lo que» without a comma, which means "the thing that": «Lo que más me gusta es el trazado».
1m9j0ic: To refer to a whole fact you need the neuter: «lo cual» or «lo que».
1nciee5: Ideas without a name: «lo + adjetivo + que», «aquello que», «eso de que»
mggx4q: «Lo + adjective or adverb + que» talks about the intensity of something: «No sabes lo bonita que está la fachada». Here the adjective agrees with the noun, even though the article is «lo»: «lo caras que son las entradas», «lo bien que lo explicó».
wn4asy: «Aquello que» and «aquello de» + infinitive refer to ideas that are distant in time or were mentioned long ago: «¿Te acuerdas de aquello de grabar de noche?». «Eso de que» + clause quotes someone else's idea, often with distance or scepticism: «No me creo eso de que nadie visita el museo». And «lo que» + subjunctive leaves the choice open: «Graba lo que te parezca interesante».

13qdzpl: Text of the first three stops of an audio guide prepared by a residents' association in La Plata. The association and the private houses are fictional.
1o0qakg: Welcome to La Plata, a city whose plan was drawn before a single house existed. In 1882, when Buenos Aires became the national capital, the province needed a new capital, and a team of engineers and architects designed it from scratch. The result is a perfect grid crossed by diagonal avenues, which lets you cross the city in a straight line and, according to the locals, get lost with surprising ease.
1w8h6dr: Our first stop is the main square, on whose sides stand the two powers of the time: the cathedral and the town hall. It is no coincidence. The founders wanted the Church and the government to face each other, so the axis joining the two buildings is also the symbolic centre of the city. Notice how tall the cathedral is: its towers were not finished until 1999, more than a century after the first stone was laid.
1vkucco: We now walk along 51st Street to a «casa chorizo» with a plain façade. Its first owners were a family of Italian engineers, whose children went on living here for seventy years. The house was about to be demolished in the nineties, to which the neighbours responded with a campaign that ended with it being declared a listed building. Today you can visit the courtyard, whose tiles are the originals.
1g6dnjr: The third stop is the station, whose platforms keep the iron roof brought from Europe. For decades the train connected the city with the national capital, so many workers lived here and commuted every day. When the service was cut back, the building was abandoned, which sparked protests from those who saw it as part of their history.
11wxp85: Before we go on, a word of warning. You may have heard the idea that in La Plata all the streets are the same. It is not entirely true: each block has its details, and the interesting thing is to discover them. We ask you to notice what does not appear in the guidebooks: a plaque, a stained-glass window, a jacaranda planted by a neighbour whose name nobody remembers.

8s7bl6: The building keeps almost intact the central dome, the tiles of the stalls and a clock whose hands stopped, so they say, on the day it closed. Notice how tall the columns are: they were designed so that the air would circulate and food would stay fresh without fridges.
3qd133: In 1978 the market closed, which left dozens of people out of work and the neighbourhood without its meeting place. The building was abandoned for twenty years, so many residents took it for granted that it would be demolished. However, an association got it declared a listed building, which was followed by a long restoration. Today it houses a farmers' market and a library. Don't believe the idea that it is just a place to shop: it is worth sitting in the upper gallery and looking at what time has not changed.
